performers: Peter Pears, tenor; Dennis Brain, horn; Boyd Neel String Orchestra; Benjamin Britten, conductor
intro: Britten’s setting of Blake’s “The Sick Rose” is one of the two songs that Boosey & Hawkes calls the centrepiece of the Serenade. Pears, Brain and the Boyd Neel String Orchestra recorded it in 1944, with Britten conducting.

sections.label: A′ · Conclusion, strings and horn
sections.mNote: The introduction’s material and the horn’s top C return.

cues.title: Introduction before the voice
cues.text: The Elegy opens with a long introduction for strings and horn. Richard Cooke hears the string accompaniment as the worm of the poem moving underground, and notes a weighty double-bass pizzicato throughout the movement.
cues.evidence: Richard Cooke, conductor, blog 16, 13 July 2020, on the Elegy: a long introduction and conclusion for strings and horn, the worm “shuffling along under the ground” in the string accompaniment, the double basses playing a weighty pizzicato throughout: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64

cues.title: Sustained top C, then B
cues.text: The horn rises to a sustained top C and slips a semitone to B. Cooke places this exposed entry in the fifteenth slow bar. Colin Clarke counts two sustained high Cs in the movement, each resolving to a held B natural; the second comes near the end.
cues.evidence: Richard Cooke, blog 16, 13 July 2020: the horn “rising with an exposed entry in the 15th slow bar on a top C” and slipping a semitone after a strong crescendo: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64 . Colin Clarke, Seen and Heard International, 11 April 2024: the Elegy “includes two sustained high C’s” resolving to a sustained top B natural: https://seenandheard-international.com/2024/04/britten-sinfonias-typically-adventurous-programme-mixing-a-world-premiere-with-music-of-today/

cues.title: Tenor enters with Blake’s poem
cues.text: The tenor enters after a quiet moment and declaims Blake’s eight lines as a recitative, against shifting chords in the strings. They run from “O Rose, thou art sick” to “Does thy life destroy”.
cues.evidence: Richard Cooke, blog 16, 13 July 2020: the soloist recites the poem as a recitative: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64 . Colin Clarke, Seen and Heard International, 11 April 2024: the tenor’s lines heard against shifting chords in the strings: https://seenandheard-international.com/2024/04/britten-sinfonias-typically-adventurous-programme-mixing-a-world-premiere-with-music-of-today/ . The poem’s eight lines: Wikipedia, Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_for_Tenor,_Horn_and_Strings

cues.title: Sackville-West on the Serenade
cues.text: Edward Sackville-West, who advised Britten on the poems and received the dedication, wrote that the cycle’s subject was night, including “the worm in the heart of the rose, the sense of sin in the heart of man”.
cues.evidence: Sackville-West’s description, quoted in Jon Kochavi’s note for the Sun Valley Music Festival, 29 July 2022: https://www.svmusicfestival.org/program_notes/program-notes-stories-and-poems/ . His advice on the poems and the dedication: Wikipedia, Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_for_Tenor,_Horn_and_Strings

cues.title: Orchestral conclusion
cues.text: After the tenor’s last line the strings and horn play an extended conclusion. Cooke hears in it the same worm music as in the introduction.
cues.evidence: Richard Cooke, blog 16, 13 July 2020: the soloist recites the poem and the orchestra then plays the extended conclusion; introduction and conclusion share the theme of the worm in the strings and horn: https://www.richardcooke.org/blogtext.htm?blog=64

cues.title: Second top C, again resolving to B
cues.text: Near the end the horn reaches a second sustained top C and again falls a semitone to a held B, the pair of notes it sounded in the introduction.
cues.evidence: Colin Clarke, Seen and Heard International, 11 April 2024: two sustained high Cs in the Elegy, each resolving to a sustained top B natural, the second the better in the performance reviewed: https://seenandheard-international.com/2024/04/britten-sinfonias-typically-adventurous-programme-mixing-a-world-premiere-with-music-of-today/

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Peter Pears (tenor), Dennis Brain (horn), Boyd Neel String Orchestra (string orchestra), Benjamin Britten (conductor)
fields.note: The Internet Archive creator field lists Pears, Brain and the Boyd Neel String Orchestra. The CHARM record names Britten as conductor, and Philip Stuart’s Decca discography lists Pears, Brain, the Boyd Neel String Orchestra and Britten for the session.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The Elegy alone, on one side of the six-side Decca set AK 1151–53: side 3 of 6, matrix AR 8463. It shares a disc with the Dirge (side 4, AR 8464).
fields.note: The titles of the six sides in the CHARM record and the Internet Archive items show the Elegy on a side of its own. That the side holds the whole movement is inferred from the neighbouring sides, which begin and end with other movements, and from the side’s length (4 min 21 s); no source states the movement’s duration in this recording or compares the side with the score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Stuart’s discography records the Serenade sessions as 25 May 1944 and says that three sides (8461, 8464 and 8466) were re-made on 8 October 1944. The side transferred here is AR 8463, take 2, which is not among the re-made sides, so it is inferred to date from 25 May 1944; the discography does not say which take was issued.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The discography lists the 25 May 1944 session at West Hampstead Studios, Decca’s London studios.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The Internet Archive item gives the label as Decca and the speed as 78; Stuart’s discography lists the Serenade among Decca’s UK 78 rpm issues. The record size is not stated in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Decca AK 1153 (third disc of the automatic-coupling set AK 1151–53), issued in the UK in November 1945
fields.note: The file name of the transfer is AK_1153_AR_8463-2. Stuart lists the issue as “(Nov45) (A)K1151-53”, and says UK release dates come from Decca’s monthly supplements or from advertisements and reviews in The Gramophone. The December 1945 issue of The Gramophone reviews the set as “Decca K1151-3 … Auto AK1151-3”. The same six sides were also issued in manual sequence as K1151–53, in which the Elegy and the Dirge share K1152 (Decca advertisement, The Gramophone, February 1946); the disc transferred here is the automatic coupling AK 1153, which carries the same two sides.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: AR 8463, take 2 (side 3 of 6); AR 8464 take 4, the Dirge, is on the other side of the same disc
fields.note: From the item metadata and the CHARM record, which list the six sides of the set as AR 8461-4, AR 8466-4, AR 8462-3, AR 8465-4, AR 8463-2 and AR 8464-4.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item names no transfer engineer. It belongs to the Internet Archive’s Centre for the History and Analysis of Recorded Music (CHARM) 78rpm collection and carries a CHARM record (METS_AK_1151, created 30 January 2009 by conversion from a spreadsheet).

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Internet Archive upload is a copying event, not the date of the transfer; the sibling item for side 4 was added on 15 January 2019.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The item states no stylus, equalisation or noise reduction. The MP3 is the Internet Archive derivative of the uploaded FLAC.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: In copyright. Britten died on 4 December 1976, so the Serenade is protected in the EU and the United Kingdom (life plus 70 years) until the end of 2046; Boosey & Hawkes is the publisher. Blake (1757–1827) wrote the poem, which is in the public domain.
fields.note: The publisher is documented by the Boosey & Hawkes page and Blake’s dates by the Sun Valley note. The term is a calculation from the composer’s death date, which the composer chapter on this site gives. Rights in the composition are separate from rights in the recording and do not block publication.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU and UK public domain: first published before 1963 (Decca AK 1151–53, November 1945). United States status not established.
fields.note: The release date is Philip Stuart’s, taken from Decca’s monthly supplements or from The Gramophone; The Gramophone for December 1945 independently reviews the set as already on sale. For a recording first published in 1945 the Copyright Office describes a term of 95 years plus 5 years after first publication in the United States, to the end of 2045; whether that term applies to this British issue was not established. The item carries no licence statement and sits in the CHARM collection, not in the Great 78 Project; its metadata carries no litigation, takedown or restriction flag.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote Grimes and Aschenbach for Peter Pears, a work with an ark full of animals for Suffolk children, and a requiem in which dead soldiers speak.
facts: Frank Bridge privately; Royal College of Music, 1930–33, with John Ireland
Lowestoft and London; North America, 1939–42; then Suffolk

composer.background:
Benjamin Britten grew up in a house facing the North Sea at Lowestoft. His father was a dentist; his mother, Edith, sang and encouraged his music. Born on St Cecilia’s Day, 22 November 1913, he learnt piano and viola and filled exercise books with compositions. At the Norwich Festival in 1924 he heard Frank Bridge conduct The Sea. In 1927 his viola teacher, Audrey Alston, introduced him to its composer.

Bridge took him on. The lessons could be uncomfortable. “I used to get sent to the other side of the room,” Britten recalled in the Sunday Telegraph in 1963; “Bridge would play what I’d written and demand if it was what I’d really meant.” In 1937 he thanked his teacher with the Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge, ten variations for strings, among them a waltz, a funeral march and a fugue.
